newsitem.title: UK: RUGBY UNION-OLD GHOSTS THREATEN ENGLISH PROGRESS.
newsitem.headline: RUGBY UNION-OLD GHOSTS THREATEN ENGLISH PROGRESS.

text.p: England still have a mathematical chance of winning the Five Nations title this weekend but must overcome numerous bad omens if Wales are to be beaten on their final appearance at the soon-to-be-demolished Cardiff Arms Park.

There will be no shortage of sentiment on Saturday as the Welsh pay their last respects to their 113-year-old home, destined to become a state-of-the-art superdome twisted at 90 degrees from the current pitch in time to host the Rugby World Cup in 1999.

But if the architects are excited about their 21st century creation, English and Welsh coaching counterparts Jack Rowell and Kevin Bowring are relying on ghosts from another era to conclude a season which has not run as smoothly as either man had planned.

Should England number 10 Mike Catt fail to last the game, the rival fly-halves would be two 34-year-olds who first played against each other for their respective countries when Welsh replacement Craig Quinnell was a nine-year-old.

Jonathan Davies and Rob Andrew, back on the English bench as emergency goalkicking cover, were both involved in 1985 on the day Davies marked his Welsh debut with a try in a 24-15 Cardiff win and Davies again finished on the winning side in the corresponding fixture two years later.

Now the former captain, who departed for rugby league in 1989, has indicated that his first Five Nations start for nine years will be his 32nd and last Welsh appearance, although he intends to use the opportunity to launch a late bid for a Lions tour place to South Africa.
Andrew is back as a "one-off" in the absence of the injured Paul Grayson, a development which Rowell's critics insist is detrimental to England's 1999 World Cup development.

Had they held on to their 20-6 lead against France at Twickenham to retain their grand slam chances, such pragmatism might have been justified against a Welsh side containing deadly goalkicker Neil Jenkins.
Instead, with a mere Triple Crown on offer unless France lose at home to Scotland, even England's players concede there is little point in a safe, unambitious conclusion to their season.
"Winning the Triple Crown counts for nothing in international terms," said flanker Lawrence Dallaglio. "It is the way the side continues to develop that is important.
"The All Blacks completely rebuilt their team after the 1991 World Cup. They lost a few games on the way but are now probably the best side in the world. England must have the same attitude.

Dallaglio, who heads off to Hong Kong on Sunday as captain of England's World Cup Sevens squad, insists the Arms Park "doesn't hold any ghosts" but the fact remains that England have won only twice in Cardiff since 1963.
Even the sight of French referee Joel Dume will unnerve them -- the only previous time he controlled the fixture, in 1993, Wales won 10-9.

Wales have had to make five enforced changes to the side who ran France to within five points in Paris and will particularly miss the cutting edge provided by Ieuan Evans and Scott Gibbs in the back-line.
But the outcome hinges on which England side they encounter -- the storming unit of the first 60 minutes against France or the hesitant outfit of the last 20 minutes.

Full-back Tim Stimpson, another man playing for a Lions place, is convinced the former will apply. "I can't wait to face the dragon," he said. "If we find ourselves 20 points up with half an hour to go there is no way we will take our foot off the gas again."
